questions.question: From the application's point of view, a database transaction reduces many different kinds of fault to which outcomes?

options.text: Commit or abort: either all of its writes take effect or none of them do
Success or automatic retry: the database keeps retrying until it succeeds
Committed, aborted, or partially applied and awaiting manual repair
One distinct outcome for each ACID property that could be violated

questions.explanation: A transaction groups several reads and writes into one logical unit that either commits (all writes take effect) or aborts (all writes are discarded). Crashes, network interruptions, full disks, constraint violations and many concurrency conflicts all surface to the application as a simple abort, after which it can safely retry. The database does not retry for you, and the whole point is that a partially applied state is never left behind.

questions.question: Which of these are real fault or concurrency hazards that database transactions help applications cope with? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The database software or hardware may fail at any time, including in the middle of a write, and the application may crash halfway through a series of operations
Network interruptions can unexpectedly cut off the application from the database, or one database node from another
Several clients may write at the same time and overwrite each other's changes, or a client may read data that has only been partially updated
Read-only queries that run at the same time as each other can permanently corrupt the data they read, even when no transaction is writing

questions.explanation: Transactions address two families of hazard: faults that interrupt a sequence of writes (database or hardware failure, application crashes, network interruptions) and concurrency problems (clients overwriting each other or seeing partially updated data). Concurrent reads of the same data, with no writer involved, do not create a race condition: races need at least one transaction modifying data that another reads or writes.

optionExplanations.a: A database or application can stop after only part of a logical operation, so transactions need a way to remove the partial writes and expose a single commit-or-abort outcome.
optionExplanations.b: A broken connection leaves the client uncertain about which operations reached the database, and a node-to-node interruption can split an operation; aborting and retrying makes this manageable.
optionExplanations.c: Concurrent clients can overwrite one another or observe a half-finished update, which is exactly the class of race condition that transaction isolation is meant to prevent.
optionExplanations.d: Reads that run alongside other reads do not modify anything, so they cannot conflict; a race condition requires a transaction that writes data another transaction is also reading or writing.

questions.question: In a database, what is a transaction?

options.text: Several reads and writes grouped into one unit that commits or aborts as a whole
A single write applied atomically to exactly one object, such as one key-value pair
A lock held on a set of rows for the entire duration of a client's connection
A durable log record that describes a change after it has been applied to disk

questions.explanation: A transaction groups several reads and writes so that, conceptually, they execute as one operation: the whole transaction commits or the whole transaction aborts. That lets the application ignore partial failure and certain concurrency issues. A single-object atomic write is useful but is not a transaction in the usual sense, and locks and logs are implementation mechanisms rather than the definition.

questions.question: What was the original purpose of database transactions?

options.text: To simplify the programming model for applications that access a database
To improve write throughput by batching many writes into one disk operation
To enable distributed consensus among the nodes of a replicated database
To satisfy audit requirements imposed on databases by financial regulators

questions.explanation: Transactions are not a law of nature; they were created to simplify the programming model. With transactions the application can ignore certain error scenarios and concurrency issues because the database handles them (these are its safety guarantees). They usually cost performance rather than improving it, and they are a general programming abstraction, not a consensus protocol or a regulatory feature.

questions.question: Does every application need transactions?

options.text: No: weakening them can buy performance or availability
Yes: every application that writes any data needs full transactions
Only applications that handle financial data genuinely need transactions
Only applications distributed across several machines need transactions

questions.explanation: Transactions are a trade-off, not a requirement. An application with very simple access patterns, such as reading and writing a single record, can often manage without them, and dropping or weakening transactional guarantees can improve performance or availability. Deciding requires knowing exactly which safety guarantees transactions provide and what they cost. The need depends on how operations interact, not on whether the data is financial or distributed.

questions.question: Where does the style of transaction support used by MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server originate?

options.text: IBM System R (1975), the first SQL database; the idea is largely unchanged
Oracle in 1985; the design has been fundamentally rewritten several times since
The 1992 SQL standard, which replaced earlier incompatible transaction designs
The 1983 paper that coined ACID, which predated any working implementation

questions.explanation: Most databases follow the transaction style introduced in 1975 by IBM System R, the first SQL database. Although implementation details changed, the general idea stayed virtually the same for about 40 years (as of the late 2010s), and transaction support in MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server is uncannily similar to System R's. The ACID acronym came later, in 1983, to describe guarantees that already existed in practice.

questions.question: In the late 2000s, which traditional database feature did many new NoSQL databases abandon or redefine to mean something much weaker?

options.text: Transactions: grouping several writes so they commit or abort together
Partitioning, by requiring every dataset to fit on a single machine
Replication, by running each database as a single unreplicated node
Flexible data models, by requiring a fixed relational schema everywhere

questions.explanation: NoSQL databases aimed to improve on relational systems by offering new data models and by including replication and partitioning by default. Transactions were the main casualty: many of these databases abandoned them or used the word for a much weaker set of guarantees. This fed the belief that transactions and scalability were fundamentally opposed.

questions.question: Two popular claims about transactions are that they are the antithesis of scalability, and that they are essential for any serious application with valuable data. Which view is most accurate?

options.text: Both are hyperbole: transactions have advantages and limitations, like any design choice
The first: any large-scale system must abandon transactions to keep good performance and availability
The second: every application holding valuable data requires full transactional guarantees
Neither applies, because transactions impose no measurable cost in modern distributed databases

questions.explanation: Both viewpoints are exaggerations. Like any technical design choice, transactions bring guarantees (atomic commit, isolation, durability) and costs (coordination, latency, sometimes availability). Large systems can use transactions, and valuable data does not automatically require the strongest guarantees; whether the cost is worth paying depends on the application's invariants and workload.

questions.question: What does the acronym ACID stand for, and who coined it?

options.text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability; coined by Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter in 1983
Atomicity, Concurrency, Isolation, Durability; coined by Jim Gray in 1981
Availability, Consistency, Isolation, Durability; coined by Edgar Codd in 1970
Atomicity, Consistency, Integrity, Durability; coined by the SQL standard committee in 1992

questions.explanation: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability. Härder and Reuter coined it in 1983 to establish precise terminology for fault-tolerance mechanisms in databases. In practice implementations diverged, especially around isolation, so an 'ACID' label alone no longer tells you exactly which guarantees a system provides.

questions.question: Why is a database's claim to be 'ACID compliant' of limited value?

options.text: Because ACID implementations differ between databases, especially isolation
Because ACID describes only single-object writes and never multi-object transactions
Because the four ACID properties are impossible to implement together in one system
Because the great majority of databases make no ACID claims at all

questions.explanation: The high-level idea of ACID is sound, but the details vary: there is a lot of ambiguity around isolation in particular, so two 'ACID' databases can permit quite different anomalies. That is why ACID has become mostly a marketing term. The properties can be implemented together, they cover multi-object transactions, and many databases do claim ACID; the problem is that the claim does not pin down the guarantees.

questions.question: What does BASE usually mean in database discussions?

options.text: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency; a vague label meaning roughly 'not ACID'
Basic Atomicity, Serializability, Eventual durability; a precisely specified weaker standard
Balanced Availability, Strong Eventual consistency; a guarantee stricter than ACID
Best Available State Estimate; a formally defined consistency model

questions.explanation: Systems that do not meet the ACID criteria are sometimes called BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency. It is even vaguer than ACID; its only sensible definition is 'not ACID', so it can mean almost anything. Two BASE systems can behave very differently, and their concrete guarantees still need to be examined.

questions.question: How does atomicity in ACID differ from 'atomic' in multi-threaded programming?

options.text: ACID atomicity means abort-and-discard on faults; threading atomicity means no visible half-done state
They mean the same thing: no other process can ever observe a half-finished operation of either kind
ACID atomicity is about concurrent access to data; the threading sense is about surviving crashes
ACID atomicity is about writing to durable storage; the threading sense is about lock-free data structures

questions.explanation: In multi-threaded programming, an atomic operation means no other thread can see its half-finished result. ACID atomicity is not about concurrency at all (that is isolation). It describes what happens when a client makes several writes and a fault occurs partway: the transaction is aborted and the database discards or undoes the writes made so far. 'Abortability' would arguably be a clearer name.

questions.question: Under ACID atomicity, a transaction that cannot complete is aborted and all its writes are discarded. Which events can force such an abort partway through a transaction? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The database process crashes after some of the transaction's writes
The network connection between client and database is interrupted
The disk becomes full, or a write violates an integrity constraint
Another client concurrently reads the rows the transaction is writing

questions.explanation: ACID atomicity covers faults that occur after some of a transaction's writes have been processed: a process crash, an interrupted network connection, a full disk, or a violated integrity constraint. In each case the database aborts the transaction and discards its partial writes so the application can safely retry. What other clients can see while the transaction runs is a separate concern handled by isolation.

optionExplanations.a: A crash can stop a transaction after only some of its writes, so atomic recovery must undo that completed prefix rather than leave it as lasting state.
optionExplanations.b: If the connection drops midway, the transaction cannot be completed, so the database aborts it and discards the writes it had already made.
optionExplanations.c: Resource exhaustion or a constraint failure rejects the transaction after work has begun, and atomicity requires the same rollback of its earlier writes.
optionExplanations.d: A concurrent read is not a fault in the transaction itself; whether that reader sees uncommitted data is an isolation question, and it does not force the writer to abort.

questions.question: Without atomicity, why is it risky for an application to retry a multi-write operation that failed partway through?

options.text: It can't tell which writes took effect, so a retry may apply some twice
A retry always fails unless the original writes were atomic in the first place
The database forbids retrying any operation that has partially failed
Retrying requires durability, which is unavailable when atomicity is absent

questions.explanation: If an error occurs partway through several changes and nothing is undone, the application does not know which changes took effect. Retrying risks making the same change twice and producing duplicate or incorrect data. With atomicity, an aborted transaction is guaranteed to have changed nothing, so the whole operation can be retried safely.

questions.question: Which term might better describe ACID atomicity, and why?

options.text: Abortability, since its defining feature is discarding all writes on error
Indivisibility, because no other transaction can observe its intermediate writes
Durability, because a transaction's committed writes survive crashes
Serializability, because transactions appear to run one at a time

questions.explanation: The defining feature of ACID atomicity is the ability to abort a transaction on error and have all of its writes discarded, so 'abortability' arguably describes it better; 'atomicity' is kept because it is the usual word. Hiding intermediate writes from other transactions is isolation, not atomicity, and surviving crashes after commit is durability.

questions.question: The word 'consistency' is overloaded in data systems. Which pairings of context and meaning are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Replication: replica consistency, including eventual consistency in asynchronously replicated systems
Consistent hashing: a guarantee that every replica of a partition holds identical data
CAP theorem: linearizability, where operations appear to take effect atomically in one order
ACID: an application-specific notion of the database being in a 'good state'

questions.explanation: 'Consistency' has at least four meanings: replica consistency (such as eventual consistency under asynchronous replication), consistent hashing (a partitioning technique used for rebalancing), linearizability in the CAP theorem, and in ACID an application-defined notion of valid data that satisfies invariants. Consistent hashing decides which node stores a key; it says nothing about replicas agreeing.

optionExplanations.a: In replication, consistency describes how replicas converge and what reads may observe, including eventual consistency when followers are updated asynchronously.
optionExplanations.b: Consistent hashing is a way of assigning keys to partitions so that rebalancing moves little data; it is not a guarantee that replicas hold identical data.
optionExplanations.c: In CAP, consistency is used as shorthand for linearizability: operations appear to take effect atomically in a single order consistent with real time.
optionExplanations.d: ACID consistency means preserving application-defined invariants, such as balanced credits and debits, rather than replica agreement or a particular isolation model.

questions.question: Who is primarily responsible for ACID consistency, that is, preserving invariants such as 'credits and debits across all accounts must balance'?

options.text: The application, which must define its transactions so they preserve its invariants
The database, which detects and rejects any write that violates any invariant
The replication layer, which makes all replicas hold the same data
The database administrator, who enforces every invariant through the schema alone

questions.explanation: ACID consistency depends on the application's notion of invariants, and it is the application's responsibility to write transactions that preserve them. The database can check some specific invariants, such as foreign key or uniqueness constraints, but in general if you write bad data that violates your invariants, the database cannot stop you. The application relies on atomicity and isolation to achieve consistency, but it is not up to the database alone.

questions.question: Why is it argued that the C doesn't really belong in ACID?

options.text: Consistency belongs to the application, while A, I and D are properties of the database
Consistency is entirely redundant with durability, so it adds nothing to the acronym
Consistency cannot be achieved by any database, even with declared constraints
Consistency is the only one of the four properties the database alone fully guarantees

questions.explanation: Atomicity, isolation and durability are mechanisms the database provides. Consistency in the ACID sense refers to application-defined invariants, which the database can only help preserve when the application uses those mechanisms correctly. Joe Hellerstein has remarked that the C was 'tossed in to make the acronym work' in Härder and Reuter's paper.

questions.question: Two clients concurrently increment a counter stored in a database. Each reads the current value (42), adds 1, and writes the result back, with no isolation and no built-in increment operation. What is the final value?

options.text: 43 rather than 44, because one increment is lost
44, because each individual write is atomic
42, because the database rejects both conflicting writes
43, and the second client receives a conflict error

questions.explanation: Both clients read 42, both compute 43, and both write 43, so the counter ends at 43 even though two increments happened. Each single write is atomic, but the read-modify-write cycle as a whole is not, and without isolation nothing detects or reports the conflict. Isolation or an atomic increment operation would make the result 44.

questions.question: How do classic database textbooks formalize transaction isolation?

options.text: As serializability: the result equals some one-after-another execution
As linearizability: every read returns the most recent write in real time
As snapshot isolation: every transaction reads from a consistent snapshot
As atomicity: every transaction's writes are either all applied or all discarded

questions.explanation: Isolation means concurrently executing transactions cannot interfere with each other. The classic textbooks formalize this as serializability: each transaction can pretend it is the only one running, and the database ensures the committed outcome equals some serial (one-at-a-time) execution, even though the transactions actually ran concurrently. Snapshot isolation is weaker, linearizability is a recency guarantee for single objects, and atomicity concerns abort on faults.

questions.question: In Oracle 11g, what does the isolation level named 'serializable' actually implement?

options.text: Snapshot isolation, which is weaker than true serializability
True serializability, implemented with two-phase locking
True serializability, implemented with single-threaded serial execution
Read committed, with a fresh snapshot taken for each query

questions.explanation: Serializable isolation carries a performance cost and is rarely used in practice; Oracle 11g does not implement it at all. Its level called 'serializable' actually provides snapshot isolation, which still permits anomalies such as write skew. This is one example of why isolation level names cannot be trusted without knowing their actual semantics.

questions.question: What does durability in ACID promise?

options.text: Committed data will not be forgotten, even after a crash or hardware fault
Written data survives in memory, so writing to disk or replicas is unnecessary
Data is written to a volatile cache before the transaction is reported committed
Committed data can always be recovered from the previous nightly backup

questions.explanation: Durability is the promise that data written by a successfully committed transaction will not be lost, even if hardware fails or the database crashes. On a single node this typically means writing to nonvolatile storage, usually with a write-ahead log for recovery; in a replicated database it may mean copying to several nodes before reporting commit. Perfect durability does not exist: if every disk and backup is destroyed, nothing can save the data.

questions.question: How has the meaning of durability in databases evolved historically?

options.text: Archive tape, then disk or SSD, and more recently replication
Writing to disk or SSD throughout, exactly as it is understood today
Replication first, then disk or SSD, and finally archive tape
In-memory persistence first, then disk, and finally archive tape

questions.explanation: Historically durability meant writing to an archive tape; then it came to mean writing to a disk or SSD; more recently it has been adapted to mean replication to other nodes. None of these is perfect: a dead machine makes its disk inaccessible, correlated faults can take out all replicas, and disks themselves fail, so robust systems combine disk writes, replication and backups.

questions.question: Which arguments bear on disk versus replication for durability? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Replication keeps committed data accessible after one machine fails
Disk can survive correlated failures that stop every replica
Disk protects writes not yet copied by asynchronous replication
Replication to other nodes makes writing to local disk entirely unnecessary

questions.explanation: Replication improves availability when one durable machine is inaccessible, while local disk can outlive correlated replica outages and protect asynchronously replicated writes. Robust systems often combine both.

optionExplanations.a: A surviving replica can immediately serve committed data when one machine is dead or inaccessible, whereas a lone durable disk may require repair before service resumes.
optionExplanations.b: Power loss, software bugs or bad inputs can stop several replicas together; durable local media may retain their state across that correlated outage.
optionExplanations.c: An asynchronous leader may acknowledge before followers receive the write, so flushing locally protects data during the replication gap.
optionExplanations.d: Replication and local disk cover different failure modes; copying to volatile or simultaneously failing replicas does not make durable local storage universally unnecessary.

questions.question: Which findings about storage hardware undercut the assumption that writing to disk guarantees durability? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: One study found that between 30% and 80% of SSDs develop at least one bad block during their first four years of operation
Magnetic hard drives have a lower rate of bad sectors than SSDs, but a higher rate of complete failure
After sudden power loss, SSDs may violate their guarantees so that even fsync is not reliable, and an unpowered SSD can lose data within weeks
Data at rest on a disk cannot become corrupted unless something overwrites it, so old backups are always trustworthy

questions.explanation: Real storage is imperfect: SSDs commonly develop bad blocks, magnetic drives fail outright more often, fsync may not work correctly after power loss, unpowered SSDs can lose data depending on temperature, and data can silently corrupt over time. There is no single technique that gives absolute durability, only risk-reduction techniques (disk writes, replication, backups) that should be used together.

optionExplanations.a: The high observed incidence of at least one bad SSD block shows that persistent media commonly develops localized faults even while the drive appears healthy.
optionExplanations.b: Different media fail differently: magnetic disks showed fewer bad sectors in the cited comparison but a higher chance of the whole device failing.
optionExplanations.c: Firmware and power-loss behavior weaken the idea that a flushed write is safe: fsync can be unreliable, and unpowered SSD retention depends on time and temperature.
optionExplanations.d: Data on disk can gradually become corrupted without detection, and if it has been corrupt for some time, replicas and recent backups may be corrupt too.

questions.question: An email app stores a denormalized count of unread messages alongside the messages themselves. When a new message arrives, which writes must happen atomically?

options.text: Inserting the new message and incrementing the unread counter
Only incrementing the counter, since the message insert is independent
Only inserting the message, since each single-object write is already atomic
Neither, because a denormalized counter can never drift from the messages

questions.explanation: Storing the unread count in a separate field speeds up reads but creates an invariant: the messages and the counter must change together. If the insert succeeds and the increment fails (or vice versa), the mailbox and counter disagree. A multi-object transaction makes both writes commit or abort together; single-object atomicity protects each write individually but not the pair.

questions.question: In an email app, a transaction inserts a new email and then increments the unread counter. Before it commits, another user sees the new email in the mailbox listing but an unread count of zero. What anomaly is this?

options.text: A dirty read: seeing another transaction's uncommitted writes
A lost update: one of two concurrent writes is overwritten
Write skew: two transactions act on an outdated premise
A durability failure: a committed write was lost in a crash

questions.explanation: The reader saw the email the writer had inserted but not yet committed, while the counter increment had not happened yet. Reading another transaction's uncommitted writes is a dirty read, and it exposes a partially updated state. Isolation would ensure the reader sees either both the email and the updated counter, or neither.

questions.question: In an email app, a transaction inserts a new email and then fails while updating the unread counter. Which ACID property ensures the inserted email is rolled back?

options.text: Atomicity: the transaction aborts and its earlier writes are undone
Durability: the inserted email is kept even though the counter failed
Isolation: other users are prevented from seeing the half-finished state
Consistency: the database automatically recomputes the counter

questions.explanation: Atomicity ensures that if an error occurs partway through a transaction, any writes it already made are undone, so the mailbox and the counter cannot get out of sync. Isolation is a different property: it controls what concurrent readers see while the transaction runs, but it does not roll anything back. The database does not know how to recompute an application's denormalized counter.

questions.question: How does a relational database typically decide which statements belong to the same transaction, and what makes that grouping fragile?

options.text: By TCP connection: statements between BEGIN and COMMIT; a dropped connection aborts
By a session cookie sent with each statement, which another client could copy and forge
By an identifier the client attaches to each statement, which is costly to track
By an entry in the lock table, which vanishes when the lock manager evicts it

questions.explanation: On a given connection, everything between BEGIN TRANSACTION and COMMIT is one transaction. If the TCP connection is interrupted, the transaction must be aborted; worse, if it drops after the client requested commit but before the acknowledgment arrives, the client cannot tell whether it committed. A transaction manager can avoid this by grouping operations with a unique transaction identifier that is not tied to one connection.

questions.question: Many nonrelational databases offer a multi-put API. Why doesn't that resolve the lack of transactions?

options.text: Because the command may succeed for some keys and fail for others
Because a multi-put is slower than issuing the writes individually
Because a multi-put cannot address more than one key at a time
It does resolve it, because a multi-put is itself a transaction

questions.explanation: Sending several operations in one request may save network round-trips, but the server can still apply only a prefix before failure. Atomicity requires an explicit guarantee that the whole batch commits or none does.

questions.question: When a client writes a single 20 KB JSON document, which guarantees do storage engines almost universally aim to provide for that one object on one node?

options.text: Atomicity and isolation for that object, via a recovery log and per-object lock
Durability only: the write survives a crash, but readers may see it half-written
Full multi-object transactions that also cover every related document
Schema consistency only: the document is validated, but a crash may leave it torn

questions.explanation: Without per-object guarantees, a dropped connection could store an unparseable 10 KB fragment, a power failure could splice old and new values together, and a concurrent reader could see a partial update. Storage engines therefore aim for atomicity (using a log for crash recovery) and isolation (using a lock on each object) at the single-object level. That is not a multi-object transaction, which groups changes to several objects.

questions.question: Which database operations let an application avoid a read-modify-write race on a single object?

options.text: Atomic increment and compare-and-set, which combine the check and the write
Bulk insert and bulk delete, which batch many writes into one request
Snapshot reads and range scans, which read a consistent version of the data
Secondary-index lookups, which locate the object more quickly

questions.explanation: If the application reads a value, computes a new one, and writes it back in separate steps, another client can change the value in between. An atomic increment performs the whole update inside the database, and compare-and-set writes only if the value has not changed since it was read. Batching writes, reading from snapshots, or faster lookups do not close that window.

questions.question: Some vendors call single-object operations 'lightweight transactions'. Why is that a misuse of the word?

options.text: Because a transaction normally groups multiple objects, not one
Because they are too slow to deserve the name transaction
Because they provide no durability for the value they write
Because they only work on a single node, never across a cluster

questions.explanation: A multi-object transaction coordinates changes to more than one independently stored row, document or index entry. A sophisticated operation on one key remains a single-object operation.

questions.question: Which cases genuinely need multi-object transactions? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Maintaining references across relational rows or graph objects
Updating several denormalized copies of one fact
Keeping records and their secondary indexes consistent
Single-key counters, which cannot otherwise be incremented safely by concurrent clients

questions.explanation: References, denormalized copies and secondary indexes span independently stored objects, so partial updates can break invariants. A single-key counter can instead use an atomic single-object operation; avoiding transactions elsewhere shifts recovery and race handling into the application.

optionExplanations.a: Foreign keys and graph edges relate separate objects, so their inserts, updates or deletes must commit together to avoid dangling or nonsensical references.
optionExplanations.b: Denormalization stores one fact in several documents; updating only some copies leaves readers with contradictory representations of the same information.
optionExplanations.c: A record and its secondary-index entries are separate objects from the transaction's perspective, so partial maintenance can make searches miss or invent records.
optionExplanations.d: One counter can be safely changed with a datastore's atomic increment operation; it does not inherently require a transaction spanning multiple objects.

questions.question: Why have many distributed datastores omitted multi-object transactions?

options.text: They are hard to implement across partitions and can hurt availability or speed
Atomicity cannot be guaranteed once a transaction's data spans several partitions
The CAP theorem rules out multi-object transactions in partitioned databases
Multi-object transactions require all the data involved to fit on one disk

questions.explanation: Coordinating a transaction across partitions is hard, and it can get in the way when very high availability or performance is required, so many distributed datastores dropped multi-object transactions. Nothing fundamentally prevents transactions in a distributed database, however; distributed transactions exist and are valuable when invariants span objects.

questions.question: How does an ACID database handle a transaction that is in danger of violating atomicity, isolation or durability partway through?

options.text: It aborts the transaction and discards its writes, never leaving it half-done
It keeps the writes that succeeded and reports to the client which ones failed
It automatically retries the failed writes until every one of them succeeds
It commits anyway and repairs inconsistencies in a background process

questions.explanation: ACID databases prefer to abandon a transaction entirely rather than let it remain half-finished, so the application can safely retry. Not all systems work this way: datastores with leaderless replication often take a best-effort approach, doing as much as they can and not undoing what they already did, which leaves error recovery to the application. The database does not retry for you.

questions.question: What do popular ORM frameworks such as Rails's ActiveRecord and Django typically do when a transaction aborts?

options.text: They raise an exception instead of retrying, discarding the user's input
They retry the transaction indefinitely, which amplifies overload when the database is busy
They silently suppress the error, so the user believes the write succeeded
They commit the writes that succeeded before the abort, leaving partial data

questions.explanation: These ORMs don't retry aborted transactions: the error typically bubbles up the stack as an exception, the user's input is thrown away, and the user sees an error message. That wastes the main benefit of aborts, which is that an aborted transaction left no changes behind and can be retried safely. Retrying still needs care (limits, backoff, only for transient errors).

questions.question: Retrying an aborted transaction isn't perfect. Which caveats apply? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If the transaction actually succeeded but the network failed while the server tried to acknowledge the commit, retrying causes it to be performed twice — unless you have an additional application-level deduplication mechanism in place
If the error is due to overload, retrying will make the problem worse, not better; you can limit the number of retries, use exponential backoff, and handle overload-related errors differently

It is only worth retrying after transient errors such as deadlock, isolation violation, temporary network interruptions and failover — after a permanent error such as a constraint violation a retry would be pointless
If the transaction is retried too quickly after an abort, its partially applied writes may still be in place, so the retry adds its writes on top of them and duplicates data

questions.explanation: Retries are safe only when the failure is transient and the whole operation is idempotent or deduplicated. A lost commit acknowledgment can repeat a successful transaction, external side effects are not rolled back, and overload-related retries need limits and backoff.

optionExplanations.a: A lost commit response creates an ambiguous outcome: rerunning a transaction that actually committed duplicates its effects unless a stable operation ID enables deduplication.
optionExplanations.b: Immediate unlimited retries add load to an already saturated system, so overload handling needs caps, exponential backoff and often a distinct error path.
optionExplanations.c: Deadlocks, failovers and brief network faults may disappear on retry, whereas the same constraint violation will deterministically fail again until input changes.
optionExplanations.d: An aborted transaction's writes have already been discarded, so even an immediate retry starts from a clean state; duplication comes only from an earlier attempt that actually committed.

questions.question: When do race conditions between database transactions come into play?

options.text: When one transaction reads or writes data that another is concurrently modifying
Whenever two transactions run at the same time, regardless of what data they touch
Only when the transactions span more than one partition
Only when the transactions run under serializable isolation

questions.explanation: If two transactions don't touch the same data, they can safely run in parallel because neither depends on the other. Concurrency issues arise only when one transaction reads data that another is concurrently modifying, or when two transactions try to modify the same data at once. Serializable isolation exists to prevent such races, not to cause them.

questions.question: Why do concurrency bugs resist testing? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Rare timing interleavings are difficult to reproduce
Other code may access the same data unexpectedly
Concurrent users can change data between operations
Test frameworks are unable to run more than one transaction concurrently

questions.explanation: Concurrency failures may require one rare instruction-level timing, disappear on retry, and involve code paths far apart in the application. Ordinary tests therefore struggle both to trigger and diagnose them.

optionExplanations.a: A harmful interleaving may occupy a tiny timing window, so thousands of ordinary test runs can pass before one rare schedule triggers the race.
optionExplanations.b: Large applications have many independent code paths touching shared records, making it difficult for one developer or test to enumerate every interaction.
optionExplanations.c: Another user's transaction can invalidate a value between an application's read and write, even when each individual code path looks correct in isolation.
optionExplanations.d: Test tools can and do run concurrent transactions; the problem is exploring and reproducing the enormous space of timing-dependent interleavings.

questions.question: What compromise do weak (nonserializable) isolation levels make?

options.text: They block some anomalies, not all, in exchange for performance
They prevent every anomaly but force all transactions to run one at a time
They prevent no anomalies at all and exist only as labels on connections
They prevent anomalies only for read-only transactions, never for writers

questions.explanation: Serializable isolation has a performance cost that many databases do not want to pay, so systems commonly use weaker levels that protect against some concurrency issues but not all. Those levels are harder to understand and can lead to subtle bugs, so an application must know which anomalies its chosen level still permits and handle them itself.

questions.question: Which real-world consequences have concurrency bugs caused by weak isolation led to? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Substantial loss of money
Investigation by financial auditors
Corruption of customer data
A regulatory ban on weak isolation levels in financial systems

questions.explanation: Weak-isolation bugs are not theoretical: they have caused large financial losses, triggered auditor investigations, and corrupted customer data. The common reply 'use an ACID database for financial data' misses the point, because many popular relational databases considered ACID also use weak isolation by default, so they would not necessarily have prevented these bugs. Developers need to understand which race conditions their isolation level allows.

optionExplanations.a: Isolation anomalies can let conflicting financial operations both succeed, for example withdrawals that overspend, producing real monetary loss.
optionExplanations.b: When recorded transactions violate financial invariants, auditors may need to investigate how supposedly valid committed data reached an impossible state.
optionExplanations.c: Concurrent operations under weak isolation can produce combinations no user intended, leaving customer records permanently corrupted even though every transaction committed.
optionExplanations.d: There is no such universal ban; databases still default to weak isolation, so preventing these bugs remains the developers' responsibility.

questions.question: What two guarantees does the read committed isolation level make?

options.text: Reads see only committed data, and writes overwrite only committed data
Reads come from a consistent snapshot, and writes never block each other
Transactions execute in a serial order, and aborts are always safe
Reads are repeatable within a transaction, and phantoms are prevented

questions.explanation: Read committed guarantees no dirty reads (you only see data that has been committed) and no dirty writes (you only overwrite data that has been committed). It does not give a consistent snapshot, so repeated reads can differ and read skew is possible. Some databases also offer read uncommitted, which prevents dirty writes but allows dirty reads.

questions.question: What is a dirty read?

options.text: Reading another transaction's written but uncommitted data
Reading a row that a committed transaction later deleted
Reading a stale value from an asynchronously updated replica
Reading two committed values that come from different points in time

questions.explanation: A dirty read occurs when a transaction sees another transaction's uncommitted writes. Read committed prevents it: writes become visible to others only when the writing transaction commits, and then all at once. For example, if x is 2 and transaction A sets x = 3 without committing, transaction B still reads 2 until A commits. Reading committed values from different moments is read skew, a different anomaly.

questions.question: Why is it useful to prevent dirty reads? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Readers could act on a transaction's partial update
Readers could observe data that is later rolled back
Dirty reads cause the stored data on disk to become corrupted
Dirty reads violate durability rather than isolation

questions.explanation: Preventing dirty reads stops clients from observing only part of a multi-object update and from acting on values that later vanish when the writer aborts. Both cases expose a state that never committed.

optionExplanations.a: An uncommitted transaction may have changed only some related objects, so a reader can make a decision from a combination that was never meant to be visible.
optionExplanations.b: If the writer aborts, every value it exposed disappears; a dirty reader may already have acted on data that never became committed truth.
optionExplanations.c: Dirty reads affect what concurrent transactions observe, not the physical integrity of bytes stored on disk; disk corruption is a different failure class.
optionExplanations.d: The anomaly concerns visibility between concurrent transactions and therefore belongs to isolation, not the durability of committed data.

questions.question: What is a dirty write?

options.text: Overwriting a value written by a transaction that has not yet committed
Overwriting a committed value with one computed from a stale read
Writing to a stale replica, so the write is later lost during failover
A write that is discarded because its transaction aborted

questions.explanation: A dirty write happens when a later write overwrites an earlier write that belongs to a transaction that has not yet committed. Read committed prevents it, usually by making the second writer wait until the first transaction commits or aborts. Overwriting a committed value computed from an old read is a lost update, which read committed does not prevent.

questions.question: On a used-car website, buying a car requires two writes: updating the listing with the buyer and sending the buyer an invoice. Alice and Bob try to buy the same car at the same time. What can go wrong if dirty writes are allowed?

options.text: The listing names Bob as the buyer while the invoice is sent to Alice
Both buyers receive invoices, and the listing records no buyer at all
The second purchase is rejected with a uniqueness-constraint error
Both transactions deadlock, and neither purchase can complete

questions.explanation: With dirty writes, each transaction can overwrite the other's uncommitted values, so the final state can mix halves of two transactions: Bob performs the winning update to the listing, Alice the winning update to the invoice. Preventing dirty writes (read committed) makes the second buyer wait for the first transaction to commit or abort, so both records end up naming the same buyer. Without locks, the transactions do not wait for each other and so cannot deadlock.

questions.question: Read committed prevents dirty writes. Why doesn't it prevent two concurrent counter increments (read, add 1, write) from losing one increment?

options.text: Because the second write comes after the first transaction commits, so it isn't dirty
Because the counter is a single object, and isolation levels govern only multi-object access
Because read committed does not actually prevent dirty writes in practice
It does prevent it; the counter race cannot occur under read committed

questions.explanation: In the counter race, both transactions read the old value; the second writes its result after the first has already committed. No uncommitted value is overwritten, so read committed sees nothing wrong, yet one increment is lost because the second write was based on a stale read. This lost update problem needs other defenses such as atomic increments, explicit locks, or automatic lost-update detection.

questions.question: As of the mid-2010s, which databases used read committed as their default isolation level?

options.text: Oracle 11g, PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2012 and MemSQL
MySQL, MongoDB and Cassandra
IBM DB2 and Riak, with PostgreSQL defaulting to serializable
SQLite and Microsoft Access, with most others defaulting to serializable

questions.explanation: Read committed is a very popular isolation level and was the default in Oracle 11g, PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2012, MemSQL and many other databases at that time. It prevents dirty reads and dirty writes but still allows read skew and lost updates, so applications running on these defaults can hit those anomalies. MySQL/InnoDB, by contrast, defaults to repeatable read.

questions.question: How do most databases prevent dirty writes?

options.text: A row-level lock taken before writing and held until commit or abort
A lock is taken only for the duration of each individual write statement
The application must explicitly lock every row it intends to write
Each write is checked at commit time, and the later writer silently wins

questions.explanation: To modify a row or document, a transaction must first acquire a lock on it and hold that lock until the transaction commits or aborts. Only one transaction can hold the lock, so another writer must wait, which means it can never overwrite uncommitted data. Releasing the lock after each statement would let another transaction overwrite the uncommitted value, and the database takes these locks automatically in read committed mode.

questions.question: Read committed could prevent dirty reads by making each reader briefly acquire the same lock a writer holds. Why do most databases avoid this approach?

options.text: Because one long write transaction would make many readers wait
Because read locks cannot be implemented efficiently on a B-tree
Because briefly acquiring read locks would frequently cause deadlocks
Because holding read locks would violate durability guarantees

questions.explanation: If readers had to take the writer's lock, a single long-running write transaction would make many read-only transactions wait until it finished. That harms read response times and is bad for operability: a slowdown in one part of an application can have a knock-on effect in an unrelated part because of lock waits. Most databases instead let readers see the old committed value.

questions.question: How do most databases actually prevent dirty reads under read committed?

options.text: They keep the old committed value and serve it to readers until commit
They take a read lock on every object that is read and hold it until commit
They abort every concurrent reader whenever a write to the same object arrives
They delay every read until no write transactions are in flight anywhere

questions.explanation: For every object being written, the database remembers the old committed value and the new value set by the transaction that holds the write lock. While that transaction is in progress, other readers are simply given the old value; only after commit do they switch to the new value. Readers never wait for writers, and they never see data that might still be rolled back.

questions.question: Alice has $1,000 split across two bank accounts of $500 each. A transaction transfers $100 from one account to the other. Under read committed, what can Alice observe if she views her balances while the transfer is being processed?

options.text: One account before the transfer and one after, so the total looks like $900
Always a correct total of $1,000, because each balance she reads is committed
A total of $1,100, as though the transfer had created money
An error instead of balances, because the accounts are locked during the transfer

questions.explanation: Alice may read the receiving account before the transfer commits ($500) and the sending account after it commits ($400), seeing a total of $900. Each value was committed when she read it, so read committed is not violated, but the two reads come from different points in time. This anomaly is read skew; snapshot isolation prevents it by having the whole transaction read from one consistent snapshot.

questions.question: Under read committed, a transaction reads one account before a concurrent transfer commits and another account after it commits, so the total appears wrong. What is this anomaly called?

options.text: Read skew, also called a nonrepeatable read
A dirty read, since one balance was not yet committed
A lost update, since the transfer overwrote a balance
Write skew, since the reader acted on an outdated premise

questions.explanation: Neither read saw uncommitted data, so it is not a dirty read, and read committed permits it. Nothing was overwritten and the reader made no write based on what it saw, so it is neither a lost update nor write skew. The problem is that the two reads observe the database at different points in time; rereading the first account would return a different value, hence 'nonrepeatable read'. Snapshot isolation prevents it by using one snapshot for the whole transaction.

questions.question: A bank customer who sees an inconsistent total because of read skew can simply reload the page a few seconds later. Which workloads cannot tolerate such temporary inconsistency? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Long-running backups that must later restore a consistent state
Analytic queries and integrity checks that scan many records
Single-key point lookups served from an in-memory cache
Atomic increments applied to a single counter column

questions.explanation: Backups and large analytic or integrity-checking scans read much of the database over a long time while writes continue. If different parts reflect different points in time, a restored backup makes the inconsistency permanent and a scan returns nonsensical results. Snapshot isolation fixes this by giving such a transaction one consistent snapshot.

optionExplanations.a: A backup can take hours while writes continue; mixing old and new versions makes an inconsistency such as vanished money permanent once that backup is restored.
optionExplanations.b: Analytics and integrity checks combine many records, so reading them at different points in time can produce totals or violations that never existed together.
optionExplanations.c: A single-key lookup has no cross-object snapshot to reconcile, and a later read simply retrieves a newer committed version.
optionExplanations.d: An atomic increment is one protected write rather than a long multi-record read, so reading different points in time is not its hazard.

questions.question: What is snapshot isolation?

options.text: Each transaction reads only data committed before it started, from one snapshot
Each statement reads the latest committed value at the moment that statement runs
Each transaction holds read locks on everything it reads until it commits
Each transaction executes serially on a single thread, so no snapshot is needed

questions.explanation: Under snapshot isolation, a transaction sees all data that was committed when it started, and keeps seeing that same data even if other transactions later change it. That makes long-running read-only queries such as backups and analytics much easier to reason about. Reading the latest committed value per statement is read committed, which permits read skew.

questions.question: How does snapshot isolation use locks, and what principle summarizes its behavior?

options.text: Write locks stop dirty writes; readers and writers never block each other
Read and write locks are both held, so readers and writers block each other
No locks are used at all; every conflict is detected only at commit time
Only table-level locks are used, so any writer blocks the entire table for readers

questions.explanation: Like read committed, snapshot isolation typically uses write locks so that one writer can block another writer of the same object. Reads require no locks. The key principle is that readers never block writers and writers never block readers, so long-running reads on a snapshot can run alongside normal writes without lock contention. Two-phase locking, by contrast, makes readers and writers block each other.

questions.question: Why does multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) keep several committed versions of an object?

options.text: Concurrent transactions may each need the database as of a different time
Because every write must be retained forever so that auditors can review it
Because each replica needs its own private copy of every version
Because indexes must always point at the oldest version of each row

questions.explanation: Under snapshot isolation, various in-progress transactions may have started at different times and each must see the state as of its own start. The database therefore keeps several committed versions of an object side by side, which is why the technique is called multi-version concurrency control. Old versions are garbage-collected once no transaction can still see them.

questions.question: In a storage engine that uses MVCC for both read committed and snapshot isolation, how do the two levels typically differ?

options.text: Read committed takes a snapshot per query; snapshot isolation uses one per transaction
Read committed uses one snapshot per transaction; snapshot isolation takes one per query
Read committed keeps four versions of each object; snapshot isolation keeps only two
Read committed uses MVCC versions, while snapshot isolation replaces them with read locks

questions.explanation: Read committed on its own needs only two versions (committed and uncommitted), but engines that support snapshot isolation usually reuse MVCC for read committed too. The difference is snapshot scope: read committed uses a separate snapshot per query, so later queries can see newer commits, while snapshot isolation fixes one snapshot for the entire transaction and so prevents read skew.

questions.question: In PostgreSQL's MVCC implementation of snapshot isolation, how are transaction IDs assigned and used?

options.text: Each gets a unique, always-increasing ID that tags every write it makes
Each transaction gets a random UUID, so the IDs can never overflow or repeat
Each transaction's ID is the node's wall-clock time at the moment it starts
Each ID is reused by the next transaction as soon as the previous one commits

questions.explanation: When a transaction starts, it receives a unique, always-increasing transaction ID (txid), and any data it writes is tagged with that ID. Visibility rules compare these IDs to decide which versions a snapshot can see. The IDs are 32-bit integers that overflow after about 4 billion transactions; PostgreSQL's vacuum process ensures that overflow does not affect the data.

questions.question: In a PostgreSQL-style MVCC table, how is the creation and deletion of a row recorded?

options.text: Rows carry created_by and deleted_by transaction IDs; a delete sets deleted_by
Each row has a version number and checksum, and a delete removes the row immediately
Each row has a lock field and a timestamp, and a delete sets the timestamp to zero
Each row has only a created_by field, and a delete appends a separate tombstone row

questions.explanation: created_by holds the ID of the transaction that inserted the row, and deleted_by is initially empty. Deleting a row does not remove it; it sets deleted_by to the deleting transaction's ID. Older snapshots can still read the row, and garbage collection removes it once no transaction can access it any more.

questions.question: In a PostgreSQL-style MVCC table, transaction 13 changes account 2's balance from $500 to $400. How is the update stored?

options.text: A delete plus a create: the $500 row marked deleted, a new $400 row added
The single row's balance field is overwritten in place from $500 to $400
A new table is created that holds only the updated balance for account 2
The $500 row is physically removed at once and only the $400 row remains

questions.explanation: An MVCC update is internally a delete and a create, so the table temporarily holds two rows for account 2: the old $500 row marked deleted by transaction 13 and a new $400 row created by transaction 13. Because nothing is overwritten in place, a transaction whose snapshot predates 13 can still read $500, which is what makes consistent snapshots possible.

questions.question: Which visibility rules does an MVCC database use so that a transaction observes a consistent snapshot? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Writes by transactions still in progress when this transaction started are ignored, even if they later commit
Writes made by aborted transactions are ignored
Writes by transactions with an earlier ID are visible even if they were still running when this one started
Writes by transactions with a later ID are ignored, whether or not they have committed

questions.explanation: At the start of each transaction the database lists transactions that are still in progress and ignores their writes; it also ignores writes by aborted transactions and by transactions with a later ID. All other writes are visible, and these rules apply to both creation and deletion. Put another way, a version is visible if its creator had committed before the reader started and it was not deleted by a transaction that had committed by then.

optionExplanations.a: A transaction in progress at snapshot time commits concurrently with the reader, not before it, so its writes must stay invisible to keep the snapshot fixed.
optionExplanations.b: Aborted writes never become part of committed history, so no consistent snapshot may expose them.
optionExplanations.c: An earlier ID is not enough: if that transaction was still in progress when the snapshot began, it is on the ignore list and its writes stay invisible.
optionExplanations.d: A later ID means the writer started after the reader, so its writes are excluded from the reader's snapshot even once committed.

questions.question: Under MVCC snapshot isolation, transaction 12 starts and reads accounts. Transaction 13 starts later, changes account 2 from $500 to $400 and commits. When transaction 12 then reads account 2, why does it still see $500?

options.text: Writes by a later-ID transaction are ignored, so 13's changes are invisible to 12
Transaction 12 holds a read lock on account 2 that blocked transaction 13's update
Transaction 13 aborted, so its update was discarded and $500 remains current
Transaction 12 started after transaction 13 committed, so it sees the old value

questions.explanation: Transaction 13 has a later ID than 12, so both its deletion of the $500 version and its creation of the $400 version are invisible to 12. Transaction 12 keeps reading the version that was current when it started. Snapshot isolation needs no read locks for this: by creating new versions instead of updating in place, the database gives each transaction a consistent snapshot with little overhead.

questions.question: How can indexes work in a multi-version (MVCC) database?

options.text: Entries point to all versions; queries filter out ones the reader can't see
Every index is rebuilt from scratch whenever a write transaction commits
Indexes point only to the newest version, so older snapshots cannot use them
Each transaction gets a private copy of the index that is discarded at commit

questions.explanation: One option is for the index to point to all versions of an object and require index queries to filter out versions the current transaction cannot see; when garbage collection removes old versions, their index entries go too. Implementations add optimizations, such as PostgreSQL avoiding index updates when versions fit on the same page. Another approach is the append-only (copy-on-write) B-tree, where each root is itself a consistent snapshot.

questions.question: How does an append-only (copy-on-write) B-tree, as used by CouchDB, Datomic and LMDB, provide consistent snapshots?

options.text: Writes copy changed pages up to a new root; old roots stay immutable snapshots
Pages are overwritten in place, with a version stamp stored on each page
The entire tree is copied in full on every write transaction to make a snapshot
Old pages are freed immediately, so no garbage collection is needed

questions.explanation: Instead of overwriting pages, a write creates new copies of every modified page and of their parents up to the root; unchanged pages are shared and stay immutable. Each write transaction (or batch) produces a new root, and a given root is a consistent snapshot of the database when it was created, so no transaction-ID filtering is needed. Old pages still need background compaction and garbage collection.

questions.question: Which vendor isolation names commonly mean snapshot isolation?

options.text: Oracle serializable; PostgreSQL and MySQL repeatable read
All vendors call it snapshot isolation; the standard defines it explicitly
Oracle calls it repeatable read and PostgreSQL calls it serializable
The SQL standard defines snapshot isolation, and vendors deviate arbitrarily

questions.explanation: The SQL standard defined repeatable read before snapshot isolation existed and did so imprecisely. Vendors mapped newer mechanisms onto old labels: Oracle calls snapshot isolation 'serializable', while PostgreSQL and MySQL call it 'repeatable read' (although MySQL's version does not detect lost updates, so by a strict definition it is weaker). Identical names therefore do not reliably imply identical guarantees.

questions.question: What is wrong with the SQL standard's definition of isolation levels?

options.text: It is ambiguous, imprecise and not implementation-independent enough
It is precise, and all implementations consistently satisfy it
It contains no definition of isolation levels at all, only of locking
It is precise, but too strict for any real database to implement

questions.explanation: The SQL standard's isolation levels are based on System R's 1975 definitions, before snapshot isolation was invented, and they are ambiguous and imprecise. As a result, databases implementing 'repeatable read' differ widely in what they guarantee, most do not satisfy the formal research definition, and IBM DB2 even uses 'repeatable read' to mean serializability.

questions.question: What is the lost update problem, and what happens to the earlier of the two writes?

options.text: Two concurrent read-modify-write cycles run; the earlier write is silently overwritten
A write is rolled back at commit time; the earlier write is discarded by the client
A replica misses a write; the earlier write is dropped from the replication log
Two transactions read the same value; the earlier write goes stale but survives

questions.explanation: Both transactions read the same old value, compute replacements, and write them. The later write overwrites the earlier result without incorporating it, so one logically successful update is silently lost.

questions.question: Which scenarios involve a read-modify-write cycle? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Incrementing a counter or changing an account balance
Editing a list inside a JSON document and saving it
Two users reading and then replacing the same wiki page
Reading a single row by its primary key with no subsequent write to it

questions.explanation: Counters, JSON edits and whole-page wiki saves all read an old value, compute a replacement and write it back. A concurrent replacement between the read and write can be silently overwritten.

optionExplanations.a: Changing a balance normally reads the old number, calculates a new number and writes it back, leaving a window in which another calculation can intervene.
optionExplanations.b: Editing one element of a stored JSON list still requires reading the document, modifying the in-memory structure and replacing the stored value.
optionExplanations.c: Each editor reads a page version and later sends a full replacement, so the later save can erase changes committed since that read.
optionExplanations.d: A read with no subsequent write does not calculate and store a replacement value, so it lacks the modify-and-write stages of the cycle.

questions.question: What is the best lost-update defense when an atomic operation exists?

options.text: Use the database's atomic update, such as SET value = value + 1
Lock the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, then update it in application code
Rely on last write wins, which keeps only the newest value
Read the value, then write it back with a compare-and-set retry loop

questions.explanation: When the update can be expressed as a database atomic operation (for example UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1), that is usually the best choice: the database performs the read-modify-write as one step, typically under an exclusive lock or on a single thread, and no application logic can forget it. Explicit locks and compare-and-set also work but are easier to get wrong and are meant for updates that atomic operations cannot express, such as arbitrary wiki edits. Last write wins does not prevent lost updates at all; it discards one of the concurrent writes.

questions.question: How are atomic update operations (such as UPDATE ... SET value = value + 1) usually implemented inside a database?

options.text: An exclusive lock on the object from read until update, or a single thread
By optimistic retry, without locking the object at any point during the update
By relying on snapshot isolation alone to order the concurrent updates
By running each update inside a two-phase commit protocol across nodes

questions.explanation: Atomic operations are usually implemented by taking an exclusive lock on the object when it is read, so no other transaction can read it until the update has been applied; this technique is sometimes called cursor stability. Another option is to force all atomic operations to execute on a single thread. Either way the read-modify-write happens as one indivisible step inside the database.

questions.question: What do ORM frameworks do to lost-update safety?

options.text: They make unsafe read-modify-write cycles easy to write by accident
They automatically convert read-modify-write cycles into atomic operations
They prevent every kind of lost update by default configuration
They have no bearing at all on whether lost updates occur

questions.explanation: An ORM may present a field assignment as one operation while actually issuing a read followed by a replacement write. Without a lock, atomic operator or version check, that hidden cycle can lose updates.

questions.question: In a multiplayer game, a move must be checked against the game's rules before a piece's position is updated. Why use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE rather than an atomic update operation?

options.text: Validating a move needs application logic no atomic operation can express
FOR UPDATE takes a fresh snapshot, so the rule check reads consistent data
FOR UPDATE replicates the lock to every node in the cluster before the check
An atomic update would work equally well, so FOR UPDATE is redundant

questions.explanation: An atomic operation is not sufficient when the update depends on logic you cannot sensibly implement as a database query, such as validating a move. Instead the application locks the rows it will update with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, so any concurrent transaction trying to read them waits until the read-modify-write cycle completes. The catch is that you must remember to add the lock everywhere it is needed.

questions.question: How does automatic lost-update detection differ from using locks or atomic operations?

options.text: It lets cycles run in parallel and aborts one that would lose an update
It forces read-modify-write cycles to run one after another using locks
It requires the database to execute all transactions serially on one thread
It silently merges the two conflicting writes into one combined value

questions.explanation: Locks and atomic operations prevent lost updates by forcing read-modify-write cycles to happen sequentially. Automatic detection instead lets them run concurrently; if the transaction manager sees that a lost update would occur, it aborts the offending transaction, which retries its cycle. Databases can check this efficiently together with snapshot isolation.

questions.question: As of the mid-2010s, which isolation levels automatically detected lost updates and aborted the offending transaction? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: PostgreSQL's repeatable read
Oracle's serializable
SQL Server's snapshot isolation level
MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's repeatable read, Oracle's serializable and SQL Server's snapshot isolation level automatically detect when a lost update has occurred and abort the offending transaction, which can then retry. MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read does not detect lost updates. Some authors argue that a database must prevent lost updates in order to qualify as providing snapshot isolation, so MySQL does not provide snapshot isolation under this definition.

optionExplanations.a: PostgreSQL repeatable read implements snapshot isolation and aborts a transaction whose update would overwrite a concurrent committed update.
optionExplanations.b: Oracle's level named serializable is snapshot-isolation-like and detects same-object write conflicts that would otherwise lose an update.
optionExplanations.c: SQL Server exposes snapshot isolation explicitly and uses update-conflict detection rather than silently accepting a stale overwrite.
optionExplanations.d: MySQL/InnoDB repeatable read can allow the stale read-modify-write pattern to overwrite a concurrent update, so it lacks this automatic protection.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of automatic lost-update detection?

options.text: It still works when code forgets a lock or an atomic operation
It is always faster than explicit locks, whatever the contention
It works across multi-leader replicas without any coordination
It never needs to abort a transaction, since conflicts are merged

questions.explanation: Lost-update detection happens automatically and requires no special database features in application code. You might forget a FOR UPDATE lock or an atomic operation and introduce a bug, but detection still catches the conflict, aborting one transaction so the application can retry. That makes it less error-prone than opt-in mechanisms.

questions.question: To prevent two users from overwriting each other's edits to a wiki page, how is compare-and-set used, and what is its caveat?

options.text: Write only if content still equals what was read; unsafe on an old snapshot
Lock the page for the entire editing session; unsafe if the session expires
Merge both users' edits automatically; unsafe if the edits overlap
Always overwrite with the latest edit; unsafe if clocks disagree

questions.explanation: Compare-and-set allows an update only if the value has not changed since you read it, for example UPDATE ... SET content = 'new' WHERE id = 1234 AND content = 'old'. If the content changed, the update has no effect and the application must retry. But if the database evaluates the WHERE clause against an old snapshot, the condition may still be true during a concurrent write, so check that your database's compare-and-set is safe.

questions.question: Why don't locks and compare-and-set prevent lost updates in databases with multi-leader or leaderless replication?

options.text: Writes occur concurrently on several nodes, so no single current copy exists
These databases replicate synchronously, so lost updates cannot occur in them
Locks are too slow there, so last write wins is used and is safe
Compare-and-set still works fine there; only explicit locks fail to work

questions.explanation: Locks and compare-and-set assume a single up-to-date copy of the data. Multi-leader and leaderless databases usually allow concurrent writes on different nodes and replicate asynchronously, so no single copy is authoritative. A common approach instead is to keep conflicting versions (siblings) and resolve or merge them afterwards with application code or special data structures.

questions.question: In a replicated database, which property of an update operation lets replicas merge concurrent updates without losing any?

options.text: Commutativity: applying the updates in any order gives the same result
Non-commutativity: the order of updates can be used to pick a single winner
Last-write-wins timestamps: only the most recent update needs to be kept
Read-only access: replicas need no merge because nothing changes

questions.explanation: Commutative operations, such as incrementing a counter or adding an element to a set, can be applied in different orders on different replicas and still converge, which is the idea behind Riak 2.0 datatypes. Last write wins, by contrast, picks one write and discards the others, so it is prone to lost updates, even though it is the default in many replicated databases.

questions.question: In a hospital on-call scheduling system, what invariant must hold when doctors give up their shifts?

options.text: At least one doctor must remain on call for each shift
Exactly two doctors must be on call at all times, with no exceptions
Doctors may never give up a shift once assigned
At most one doctor may be on call for any shift

questions.explanation: The hospital tries to have several doctors on call but absolutely must have at least one. A doctor may give up a shift (for example when sick) provided at least one colleague remains on call. This rule spans several doctors' rows, which is what makes it vulnerable to write skew when two doctors leave at the same time.

questions.question: Alice and Bob are the only two doctors on call for a shift. Both click 'go off call' at the same time. Under snapshot isolation, each transaction checks that at least two doctors are on call, then updates its own doctor's record. What happens?

options.text: Both see 2 and update different rows, so both commit and none is on call
One check returns 2 and the other 1, so only Alice goes off call
Both checks see 1, so neither doctor is allowed to go off call
Snapshot isolation detects the conflict and aborts the second transaction

questions.explanation: Each transaction reads from a snapshot in which both doctors are on call, so both checks return 2. Alice's transaction updates Alice's row and Bob's updates Bob's, so there is no write-write conflict for snapshot isolation to detect, and both commit. The 'at least one on call' invariant is now violated: this is write skew.

questions.question: Two doctors concurrently take themselves off call after each checks that another doctor is still on call. Why is the resulting anomaly neither a dirty write nor a lost update?

options.text: Because the two transactions update two different rows
Because neither transaction writes anything
Because both transactions update the very same row
Because the two transactions happened to run serially anyway

questions.explanation: Dirty writes and lost updates involve two transactions writing the same object. Here each transaction updates a different row (its own doctor's record), so neither kind of conflict occurs. It is still a race condition, called write skew: had the transactions run one after the other, the second doctor would have been prevented from going off call.

questions.question: How does write skew relate to the lost update problem?

options.text: Write skew generalizes it: the transactions may update different objects
Write skew is a special case of it in which both transactions write the same object
They are unrelated: write skew involves only reads, lost updates only writes
Write skew is a special case of dirty reads in which uncommitted data is read

questions.explanation: Write skew can occur when two transactions read the same objects and then update some of them, possibly different ones. In the special case where they update the same object, you get a dirty write or lost update depending on timing.
