So lost updates are the narrower case, and write skew is harder to prevent because the conflicting writes may touch different objects.

questions.question: As of the mid-2010s, which of these automatically prevented write skew: PostgreSQL's repeatable read, MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read, Oracle's serializable, and SQL Server's snapshot isolation?

options.text: None; write skew was not automatically detected by these levels
All four, because each aborts conflicting concurrent writers
Only Oracle's serializable, since it is named serializable
Only PostgreSQL's repeatable read, using its lost-update check

questions.explanation: These are all snapshot-isolation levels, and the lost-update detection some of them provide only looks at transactions writing the same object. Write skew involves writes to different objects, so none of them detect it. Automatically preventing write skew requires true serializable isolation; otherwise the application must lock the rows it depends on.

questions.question: Could an ordinary database constraint enforce the rule that at least one doctor is always on call for a shift?

options.text: Not easily: it needs a multi-row constraint, which most lack
Yes: a uniqueness constraint on the shift ID is sufficient
Yes: a foreign key from each doctor to the shift is sufficient
Yes: a CHECK constraint on each doctor's row is sufficient

questions.explanation: Uniqueness, foreign key and single-row CHECK constraints each look at one row or one value. 'At least one doctor on call' is a condition over several rows, and most databases lack built-in multi-object constraints, though triggers or materialized views may emulate them in some databases. Without serializable isolation, the practical fallback is to lock the rows the decision depends on with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

questions.question: A meeting-room booking transaction checks for existing bookings of room 123 overlapping noon to 1 p.m. and inserts a booking if none exist. Under snapshot isolation, why can two such transactions both commit overlapping bookings?

options.text: Each finds no overlap in its snapshot and inserts a separate row
One transaction's insert overwrites the other's booking, a lost update
Each reads the other's uncommitted insert and ignores it, a dirty read
They cannot: snapshot isolation always rejects the second overlapping insert

questions.explanation: Both transactions check their snapshots, find no overlapping booking, and insert separate rows. They never write the same object, so snapshot isolation sees no conflict, and the 'no double booking' rule is violated. Locking the rows returned by the check doesn't help because the check returned no rows; preventing this needs serializable isolation (or a mechanism that can lock a search range).

questions.question: In an online game, a row lock prevents two players from moving the same piece at once. Yet two players concurrently move two different pieces onto the same board square. What anomaly is this?

options.text: Write skew
A dirty read
A lost update
A deadlock

questions.explanation: Each move checks that the square is empty and then updates a different piece's row, so the per-piece lock and same-object conflict detection do not fire. Both commit and the rule 'one piece per square' is violated, which is write skew. Depending on the rule, a unique constraint on position might prevent it; otherwise serializable isolation is needed.

questions.question: Two users try to register the same username at the same time; each transaction checks that the name is free and then inserts an account. What is the simplest way to prevent duplicate usernames?

options.text: A unique constraint on username, so the second insert aborts
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the existing row with that username
Running both transactions under snapshot isolation
Last write wins, so only the later registration is kept

questions.explanation: Check-then-insert is unsafe under snapshot isolation because both checks can find no existing row. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE has nothing to lock when the name is not yet taken. A unique constraint solves it directly: the database lets only one insert with that username succeed and aborts the other for violating the constraint.

questions.question: A points service lets users spend points by inserting a tentative spending item, then summing all of the user's items to check that the balance is still positive. How can write skew cause double-spending?

options.text: Each snapshot misses the other's item, so both checks pass and they overspend
One transaction's balance update overwrites the other's, a lost update
One transaction reads the other's uncommitted item and miscounts, a dirty read
It cannot: snapshot isolation aborts the second spending insert automatically

questions.explanation: Each transaction's snapshot excludes the other's concurrently inserted item, so each check sees enough points and both commit. The two inserts are different rows, so there is no write-write conflict, yet together they push the balance negative. This is write skew; serializable isolation or materializing the conflict on a lockable row prevents it.

questions.question: For which write-skew scenarios is a simple uniqueness-style database constraint a workable fix? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Two users claiming the same username: a unique constraint on the username
Two players moving pieces onto the same square, under a one-piece-per-square rule: a unique constraint on the occupied position
Two doctors going off call and leaving none: a single-row constraint on each doctor's record
Two overlapping room bookings: a uniqueness constraint on room_id alone

questions.explanation: A unique constraint directly handles duplicate usernames and, depending on the rule, can encode 'one piece per square'. It cannot express 'at least one doctor remains on call', which involves several rows. A uniqueness constraint on room_id alone would forbid every booking after the first, rather than only overlapping time ranges.

optionExplanations.a: A unique index on username gives the database one concrete value to serialize on, so only one of the concurrent claimants can commit.
optionExplanations.b: Some game rules, such as at most one piece per square, map to a unique constraint on the position; other rules may not, so this works only sometimes.
optionExplanations.c: The invariant concerns how many of several rows remain on call; a constraint that looks at one doctor's row at a time cannot see the other doctor.
optionExplanations.d: A unique room_id would allow only one booking for that room ever; preventing overlapping time ranges needs a range or exclusion constraint, range locks or serializability.

questions.question: Which sequence characterizes a write-skew transaction?

options.text: Read a precondition, decide, then write data that changes it
Lock the rows, write the change, then commit the transaction
Begin the transaction, write, then roll the change back
Read the value, merge it locally, then retry the write

questions.explanation: The shared pattern is a decision made from a predicate followed by a write that changes that predicate. Under snapshot isolation, two transactions can make compatible-looking decisions from old snapshots and commit disjoint writes.

questions.question: Write skew follows a pattern: a SELECT checks whether a condition holds, the application decides to proceed, and it writes. Which statements correctly describe how that write changes the condition that was checked? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Re-running the original SELECT after the write commits would return a different result
In the on-call example, there is now one fewer doctor on call
In the room-booking example, the room is now booked for that time
The rows matched by the SELECT are unchanged; only their transaction IDs differ

questions.explanation: The write changes the set of rows matching the search condition, so the precondition of the decision is no longer what it was: a doctor has left, a room has become booked, a username or square has become taken, an account has less money. A concurrent transaction that checked the same condition on an older snapshot is now acting on an outdated premise. Transaction IDs are bookkeeping, not the application's condition.

optionExplanations.a: The write changes which rows satisfy the search, so repeating the check after commit gives a different answer, which proves the decision depended on a changed premise.
optionExplanations.b: Taking a doctor off call reduces the count that the on-call check relies on, invalidating a concurrent transaction's earlier observation of two doctors.
optionExplanations.c: Inserting a booking turns an apparently free time slot into an occupied one, so a concurrent check that found no overlap is now outdated.
optionExplanations.d: The write really does change which rows match the condition; transaction IDs help implement visibility but are not the condition the application checked.

questions.question: Why can't SELECT ... FOR UPDATE prevent write skew when a transaction checks for the absence of matching rows (such as no overlapping booking) before inserting one?

options.text: The check returns no rows, so there is nothing to attach a lock to
FOR UPDATE can lock only rows in tables other than the one being inserted into
FOR UPDATE cannot be used in a transaction that also performs an insert
The insert does not count as a write from the database's point of view

questions.explanation: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the rows a query returns. In the doctor example the rows later modified were among those returned, so locking them works. But when the check is for the absence of rows and the write inserts a new matching row, the query returns nothing and no lock is taken. A write that changes another transaction's search result like this is called a phantom.

questions.question: In transaction isolation, what is a phantom?

options.text: A write that changes another transaction's search result
A write by an aborted transaction that nonetheless remains visible
A stale value read from a lagging asynchronous replica
A deadlock between two transactions searching the same table

questions.explanation: A phantom occurs when one transaction's insert, update or delete changes which rows match another transaction's search condition. Snapshot isolation avoids phantoms in read-only queries because they read a fixed snapshot, but in read-write transactions phantoms can cause write skew, as in double bookings. Preventing them requires something that covers rows that don't exist yet, such as predicate or index-range locks.

questions.question: What does 'materializing conflicts' mean for a meeting-room booking system?

options.text: Pre-creating rows per room and 15-minute slot for bookings to lock
Adding a trigger that rejects any booking overlapping an existing one
Running all booking transactions serially on a single dedicated thread
Storing each booking twice so that a duplicate reveals a conflict

questions.explanation: The phantom problem is that there is no existing object to lock. Materializing conflicts introduces lock objects artificially: a table with one row per room and time period (say 15 minutes), created ahead of time. A booking transaction locks the rows for the room and period it wants, then checks for overlaps and inserts. The extra table stores no booking data; it only turns the phantom into a lock conflict on concrete rows.

questions.question: How should materializing conflicts be regarded as a way to prevent write skew?

options.text: As a last resort, since it is error-prone and pollutes the data model
As the recommended default approach for most applications with invariants
As always preferable to using a serializable isolation level instead
As required whenever phantoms are theoretically possible in a schema

questions.explanation: Figuring out how to materialize conflicts can be hard and error-prone, and it is ugly to let a concurrency control mechanism leak into the application's data model. For those reasons it should be a last resort when no alternative is possible; a serializable isolation level is much preferable in most cases.

questions.question: Why is relying on weak isolation levels unsatisfying in practice? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Isolation levels are hard to understand and inconsistently implemented in different databases — for example the meaning of 'repeatable read' varies significantly

If you look at your application code it's difficult to tell whether it is safe to run at a particular isolation level, especially in a large application where you might not be aware of all the things that may be happening concurrently

There are no good tools to help us detect race conditions: static analysis tools may help, but they have not yet found their way into practical use, and testing for concurrency issues is hard because they are usually nondeterministic

The problem is entirely new: weak isolation anomalies only appeared once databases began replicating and partitioning data across several machines, so the single-node relational systems that came before were never exposed to them

questions.explanation: Isolation levels are hard to understand and inconsistently implemented, it is hard to tell from application code whether it is safe at a given level, and there are no good tools for detecting race conditions, which are nondeterministic and hard to test. This is not new: weak isolation levels date back to the 1970s on single-node systems, and researchers' answer has always been to use serializable isolation.

optionExplanations.a: Names such as repeatable read map to different guarantees across vendors, so transferring an application can silently expose anomalies its developers thought were prevented.
optionExplanations.b: Safety depends on every concurrent access path and shared invariant, which is difficult to infer by inspecting one function in a large codebase.
optionExplanations.c: Race detectors for database isolation are not yet routine, and nondeterministic timing makes ordinary tests poor at proving the absence of anomalies.
optionExplanations.d: Weak isolation and its anomalies date back to early single-node relational systems; distribution made some problems more visible but did not create them.

questions.question: What does serializable isolation guarantee?

options.text: That the result matches some serial, one-at-a-time order of the transactions
Only that every read comes from one consistent snapshot of the data
That no transaction will ever need to be aborted and retried
That every committed write survives crashes and hardware faults

questions.explanation: Serializable isolation guarantees that even though transactions may execute in parallel, the end result is the same as if they had executed one at a time in some serial order. So if each transaction is correct when run alone, it remains correct when run concurrently: the database prevents all possible race conditions. It says nothing about never aborting (implementations do abort) and durability is a separate property; consistent snapshots alone are snapshot isolation, which is weaker.

questions.question: Which three techniques do most databases that provide serializability use?

options.text: Serial execution, two-phase locking, and serializable snapshot isolation
Quorum reads, version vectors, and conflict-free replicated datatypes
Snapshot isolation, read committed, and read uncommitted
Two-phase commit, distributed consensus, and leader election

questions.explanation: Serializability is implemented by literally executing transactions one at a time, by two-phase locking (for decades the only viable option), or by optimistic concurrency control such as serializable snapshot isolation (SSI). The other options are replication or distributed-coordination techniques, or weaker isolation levels.

questions.question: What is actual serial execution, and why is the isolation it provides serializable by definition?

options.text: Running one transaction at a time on one thread, so nothing interleaves
Running transactions in parallel but committing them strictly in ID order
Running each transaction on its own thread, coordinated by row locks
Batching transactions together and applying each batch atomically

questions.explanation: The simplest way to avoid concurrency problems is to remove concurrency: execute one transaction at a time, in serial order, on a single thread. Because transactions cannot interleave, the result is by definition the same as a serial execution, and the database sidesteps detecting and preventing conflicts altogether. Committing parallel transactions in order does not stop their reads and writes from interleaving.

questions.question: When did database designers decide a single-threaded execution loop was feasible?

options.text: Around 2007
In 1975, with System R
In 1999, with the SQL/PSM standard
In 2015, with the rise of in-memory databases

questions.explanation: For decades, multi-threaded concurrency was considered essential for good performance, because transactions often waited on slow disk I/O. Only around 2007 did database designers conclude that a single-threaded loop for executing transactions was feasible: with the active data in memory and short OLTP transactions, avoiding coordination can make one serial thread faster than a heavily contended multi-threaded design. System R (1975) used locking, and in-memory databases were already established well before 2015.

questions.question: Which developments made single-threaded transaction execution viable? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Active datasets increasingly fit in inexpensive RAM
OLTP transactions are usually short and touch little data
Read-only analytics can run on snapshots outside the serial loop
CPU clock speeds increased dramatically after 2007, making threads unnecessary

questions.explanation: Two developments drove the rethink around 2007: RAM became cheap enough to keep the entire active dataset in memory, so transactions no longer wait for disk, and designers recognized that OLTP transactions are usually short with few reads and writes, while long analytic queries can run on a snapshot outside the serial loop. Single-core clock speeds did not take off; it was memory and workload shape that changed.

optionExplanations.a: When the active working set resides in RAM, a serial transaction avoids disk waits that would otherwise leave the single execution thread idle.
optionExplanations.b: Short OLTP transactions finish quickly enough that one transaction does not monopolize the serial loop for an unacceptable period.
optionExplanations.c: Long analytical reads can use a consistent MVCC snapshot outside the write-serialization loop, preventing them from blocking short OLTP work.
optionExplanations.d: CPU frequency growth stalled rather than accelerating dramatically; serial execution became viable through memory and workload changes, not faster single cores.

questions.question: In serial-execution databases such as VoltDB, what limits transaction throughput?

options.text: One CPU core per partition, plus costly coordination for cross-partition work
Disk bandwidth, because each transaction must read its data from disk
Network round-trips between the application and the database for every statement
Lock contention among the many threads executing transactions

questions.explanation: VoltDB/H-Store, Redis and Datomic execute transactions serially. That avoids locking overhead, but a single-threaded executor is capped at one CPU core. Partitioning gives each core its own partition and lets throughput scale, but transactions that touch several partitions must be coordinated across them and are far slower. Data lives in memory and transactions are submitted as stored procedures, so disk and network round-trips are not the bottleneck.

questions.question: What did database designers originally intend a transaction to encompass?

options.text: An entire flow of user activity, such as booking a flight
A single row update, exactly as in a modern web application
A batch of writes applied together overnight
One segment of the database's replication log

questions.explanation: Early database designers hoped a transaction could cover a whole multi-stage flow of user activity, such as searching for flights, choosing an itinerary, booking seats, entering passenger details and paying, all committed atomically. The idea failed because humans are slow to decide and respond: the database would have to support a huge number of concurrent, mostly idle transactions, which most databases cannot do efficiently. Modern OLTP applications therefore keep transactions short, typically within one HTTP request.

questions.question: What is the usual transaction boundary in a web application?

options.text: A transaction commits within one HTTP request
A transaction spans the user's entire browsing session
A transaction spans a whole day of a user's activity
A transaction spans one TCP connection, however many requests

questions.explanation: Web applications avoid holding a transaction open while a human thinks: a transaction is committed within the same HTTP request, and a new request starts a new transaction. Spanning a browsing session or a day would leave huge numbers of idle transactions holding resources, and transactions are not tied to a TCP connection's lifetime across many requests.

questions.question: Why does the interactive client/server style make serial execution unusable?

options.text: Because most time is spent in network round-trips
Because interactive transactions cannot be aborted
Because interactive transactions cannot be logged
Because interactive transactions violate isolation

questions.explanation: A serial execution thread cannot switch to another transaction while waiting for application decisions over the network. Stored procedures send the whole transaction logic in advance, keeping the execution loop busy.

questions.question: What do single-threaded serial-execution databases require instead of interactive multi-statement transactions?

options.text: The whole transaction, submitted in advance as a stored procedure
The application sends each statement separately and waits for each result
The client holds a database lock for the duration of the user's session
The transaction is split across several threads that run in parallel

questions.explanation: In an interactive transaction the database would sit idle waiting for the application's next statement, and with only one thread every other transaction would wait too. So these systems disallow interactive multi-statement transactions: the application submits the entire transaction code as a stored procedure, which runs quickly when all needed data is in memory.

questions.question: Why have stored procedures gained a somewhat bad reputation? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Vendor-specific languages often lack modern tooling and libraries
Database code is harder to debug, deploy, test and monitor
A slow procedure can harm every application sharing the database
Stored procedures are not part of any published database standard

questions.explanation: Traditional stored-procedure languages are vendor-specific and often lack modern libraries and tooling. Database-resident code is also harder to test, deploy, debug, and monitor, and a poorly written procedure can monopolize a shared database.

optionExplanations.a: PL/SQL, T-SQL and similar vendor languages tie code to one database and often lack the libraries and developer ecosystem of general-purpose languages.
optionExplanations.b: Code deployed inside a database fits less naturally into ordinary version control, testing, debugging, deployment and metrics workflows.
optionExplanations.c: One database instance is often shared by many application servers, so a CPU- or memory-heavy procedure degrades the shared bottleneck for every caller.
optionExplanations.d: Stored procedures have been part of the SQL standard (SQL/PSM) since 1999; the objections are about languages, tooling and operational risk, not missing standardization.

questions.question: Which languages do modern stored-procedure systems use?

options.text: VoltDB uses Java or Groovy, Datomic Java or Clojure, Redis Lua
All three of them use PL/SQL for stored procedures
VoltDB uses Lua, Datomic uses Groovy, and Redis uses Java
All three of them use Microsoft's T-SQL dialect

questions.explanation: VoltDB supports Java or Groovy, Datomic Java or Clojure, and Redis Lua. These familiar languages reduce some tooling objections, while in-memory execution keeps short serial procedures fast.

questions.question: Why does VoltDB require its stored procedures to be deterministic?

options.text: Each replica re-runs the same procedure, so the results must match
So that secondary indexes can be rebuilt from the procedure's return value
So that procedures can execute on any partition, in any order, with any timing
So that backups can be restored without needing any write-ahead log at all

questions.explanation: Instead of copying a transaction's writes to other nodes, VoltDB executes the same stored procedure on each replica. That only works if every replica produces the same result, so procedures must be deterministic; for example, a procedure needing the current date and time must use special deterministic APIs. Nondeterminism such as random numbers or wall-clock reads would make replicas diverge.

questions.question: In a partitioned serial-execution database such as VoltDB, why are cross-partition transactions much slower than single-partition ones?

options.text: They must run in lock-step across every partition they touch
They must read from disk, while single-partition transactions stay in memory
They are executed with two-phase locking instead of serially on one thread
They are retried until every partition they touch happens to be idle

questions.explanation: If each transaction stays within one partition, each partition's thread runs independently and throughput scales with the number of cores. A transaction touching several partitions must be coordinated, with its stored procedure performed in lock-step across all of them to preserve serializability. VoltDB reported only about 1,000 cross-partition writes per second, orders of magnitude below single-partition throughput, and adding machines did not raise it.

questions.question: Within which constraints is serial execution viable? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Every transaction must be small and fast, because it takes only one slow transaction to stall all transaction processing

It is limited to use cases where the active dataset can fit in memory; rarely accessed data could potentially be moved to disk, but if it needed to be accessed in a single-threaded transaction the system would get very slow
Write throughput must be low enough to be handled on a single CPU core, or else transactions need to be partitioned without requiring cross-partition coordination
Cross-partition transactions are impossible, so the dataset has to partition perfectly along transaction boundaries

questions.explanation: Cross-partition transactions are possible but must coordinate multiple serial loops, imposing a throughput ceiling. If required data is off-memory, anti-caching can abort, fetch it asynchronously, and restart rather than blocking the partition thread.

optionExplanations.a: One slow transaction blocks every transaction queued behind the same serial executor, so each transaction must complete in a small, predictable amount of time.
optionExplanations.b: A cache miss to disk would stall the only execution thread; keeping active data in memory avoids that pause, while anti-caching can fetch and restart.
optionExplanations.c: One core limits a partition's write rate, so higher throughput requires independent partitions whose common transactions do not need coordination.
optionExplanations.d: Transactions may span partitions, but coordinating their serial executors is much slower; perfect partition locality is desirable rather than an absolute requirement.

questions.question: For roughly how long was two-phase locking the only widely used algorithm for serializability in databases?

options.text: Around 30 years
Around 10 years
Around 5 years
Around 50 years, up to the present day

questions.explanation: Two-phase locking (2PL) was the only widely used serializability algorithm for about 30 years, until alternatives such as practical serial execution (around 2007) and serializable snapshot isolation (first described in 2008) appeared. Despite the similar name, 2PL is unrelated to two-phase commit (2PC), which is a distributed atomic-commit protocol.

questions.question: Which blocking rules define two-phase locking (2PL) for serializability?

options.text: Readers block writers of an object; writers block readers and writers
Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers, as in MVCC
Only writers block other writers; readers are never blocked by anyone
Locks are held only while each individual statement executes

questions.explanation: Under 2PL, several transactions may read an object concurrently, but writing requires exclusive access: if A has read an object, B must wait to write it, and if A has written it, B must wait to read it. Writers block readers and readers block writers, which is the opposite of snapshot isolation's 'readers never block writers, writers never block readers'. Because 2PL is serializable, it prevents lost updates and write skew.

questions.question: At the time of writing (mid-2010s), where was two-phase locking used to implement isolation in mainstream databases?

options.text: MySQL/InnoDB and SQL Server serializable; DB2 repeatable read
The read committed default level in PostgreSQL and Oracle
The snapshot isolation level in SQL Server, and nowhere else
Nowhere: it remained a purely academic technique

questions.explanation: 2PL implemented the serializable isolation level in MySQL (InnoDB) and SQL Server, and the repeatable read level in IBM DB2, where 'repeatable read' means serializability. PostgreSQL and Oracle default to read committed implemented with MVCC, and SQL Server's snapshot isolation is also multi-version rather than lock-based.

questions.question: How do shared and exclusive locks behave under two-phase locking?

options.text: Reads take shared locks, writes exclusive ones, held until transaction end
There is only one mode, exclusive, used for both reads and for writes
Locks are released after each statement and are reacquired as needed
Shared locks block each other, while exclusive locks never block anything

questions.explanation: A reader acquires the lock in shared mode, and many transactions may hold it in shared mode at once; a writer needs exclusive mode, which excludes all other holders. A transaction that reads then writes may upgrade its shared lock to exclusive. Locks are held until commit or abort, which gives the name: locks are acquired in the first phase (while executing) and all released in the second (at the end).

questions.question: How is a two-phase-locking deadlock resolved?

options.text: The database aborts one participant; the application retries it
The application detects the deadlock and the database retries the loser
Deadlock cannot arise under two-phase locking by construction
Deadlocks resolve themselves after a timeout without any abort

questions.explanation: Waiting cannot resolve a lock cycle because each transaction needs the other to proceed first. The database chooses a victim and aborts it to release its locks; retry policy remains the application's responsibility.

questions.question: What is the main downside of two-phase locking?

options.text: Performance: blocking causes low concurrency and unstable latency
Durability: writes may be lost on deadlock abort
Correctness: 2PL does not actually provide serializability
Complexity: 2PL is hard to implement, but performance is fine

questions.explanation: Lock bookkeeping has overhead, but blocking is the larger cost. One slow transaction can hold locks needed by many others, creating queues; deadlock aborts then waste completed work and add retry load.

questions.question: Under two-phase locking, why is there no limit on how long a transaction may have to wait for a lock?

options.text: Traditional databases don't cap transaction duration, so queues can grow
Each transaction has a hard 30-second timeout that is frequently exceeded
Detecting a deadlock always takes longer than the transaction itself
Waiting transactions are served in random rather than first-come order

questions.explanation: Traditional relational databases were designed for interactive applications that wait for human input, so they don't limit how long a transaction may run. When one transaction waits on another, there is therefore no bound on the wait, and even with short transactions a queue can form behind a contended object. This is why 2PL latencies can be unstable and very slow at high percentiles.

questions.question: What latency behavior does two-phase locking tend to show when the workload has contention?

options.text: Unstable latencies that are very slow at high percentiles
Latencies are stable, but uniformly higher than under weak isolation
Latencies are entirely unaffected by contention in the workload
Latencies suffer at the median but not at the higher percentiles

questions.explanation: Under 2PL a transaction can wait behind another that is itself waiting, so queues form and latencies are unstable, with very slow high-percentile response times under contention. One slow transaction, or one that touches a lot of data and acquires many locks, can make the rest of the system grind to a halt. Deadlocks are also more frequent than under weaker lock-based levels, and each abort wastes work that must be redone.

questions.question: Under two-phase locking, how can phantoms (writes that change another transaction's search results) be prevented?

options.text: Lock the search condition (a predicate lock) or an index range covering it
Detect deadlocks with a wait-for graph and abort one of the transactions
Apply compare-and-set to each row the search returned
Take shared locks only on the rows that the search actually returned

questions.explanation: A serializable database must stop other transactions from inserting or updating rows that would match a search another transaction has made, for example a booking for the same room and overlapping time. Locking only returned rows misses rows that don't exist yet. A predicate lock attaches to all objects matching the search condition, including future ones; index-range locks approximate it more cheaply.

questions.question: What key property distinguishes a predicate lock from an ordinary row lock?

options.text: It also covers matching objects that don't exist yet
It is always cheaper to acquire and to check than an ordinary row lock
Two predicate locks can never conflict with one another, whatever they cover
It applies only to rows that already exist in the table when it is taken

questions.explanation: A predicate lock belongs to all objects matching a search condition (for example, bookings of room 123 between noon and 1 p.m.), not to one particular row. Because it covers objects that might be inserted later, it prevents phantoms; with predicate locks, two-phase locking prevents all forms of write skew and becomes serializable. The downside is cost: checking many active predicate locks is slow.

questions.question: Why do most two-phase-locking databases implement index-range locks instead of true predicate locks?

options.text: Predicate locks are slow to check; index ranges are cheaper but lock more than needed
Index-range locks are more precise, locking fewer objects than the predicate would
Predicate locks cannot prevent phantoms, whereas index-range locks can
Index-range locks remove the need for any shared locks at all

questions.explanation: Predicate locks perform poorly because checking every write against many active predicates is time-consuming. Index-range locking (also called next-key locking) approximates the predicate by locking a broader set, such as all bookings for room 123, or all rooms between noon and 1 p.m. That is safe because any write matching the original predicate also matches the approximation, and it has much lower overhead.

questions.question: For a query on bookings of room 123 between noon and 1 p.m., where can a two-phase-locking database attach an index-range lock, and what is the fallback without a suitable index?

options.text: On the room_id entry or a time-index range; else a whole-table lock
On each row the query returned; otherwise no lock is taken at all
On the client's network connection; otherwise the query simply times out
On the transaction's own ID; otherwise the transaction is aborted

questions.explanation: If the query uses an index on room_id, the database can attach a shared lock to the entry for room 123; if it uses a time index, it can lock the range of values overlapping noon to 1 p.m. Any transaction inserting or changing a matching booking must update that part of the index and so hits the lock. With no suitable index, the database can fall back to a shared lock on the entire table, which is safe but blocks all writers to it.

questions.question: What problem motivated serializable snapshot isolation (SSI)?

options.text: Serializability performed or scaled badly; weak levels allowed races
Weak isolation levels were too slow for read-heavy analytic workloads
Two-phase locking failed to provide true serializability in practice
Serial execution allowed write skew whenever contention was high

questions.explanation: Two-phase locking provides serializability but performs poorly, and serial execution doesn't scale beyond one core per partition. Weak isolation levels perform well but allow lost updates, write skew and phantoms. SSI was proposed to offer full serializability with only a small performance penalty compared with snapshot isolation.

questions.question: How does serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) compare with plain snapshot isolation?

options.text: It provides full serializability with only a small performance penalty
It provides the same guarantee as snapshot isolation but runs faster
It provides serializability, but blocks readers like two-phase locking
It provides weaker guarantees than snapshot isolation in order to reduce aborts

questions.explanation: SSI adds conflict detection to snapshot isolation, giving full serializability with only a small performance cost and without blocking readers. It was first described in 2008 (Michael Cahill's PhD research), has been PostgreSQL's serializable level since version 9.1, and a similar algorithm is used by FoundationDB. At the time of writing it was still young and proving its performance in practice.

questions.question: Why is two-phase locking called a pessimistic concurrency control mechanism?

options.text: When another lock signals possible trouble, it waits until it is safe
It lets transactions proceed and checks for conflicts only at commit
It predicts conflicts from timestamps without ever taking any locks
It assumes conflicts are rare and aborts transactions only when they commit

questions.explanation: 2PL follows the principle that if anything might possibly go wrong (indicated by a lock held by another transaction), it is better to wait until the situation is safe before doing anything, much like mutual exclusion in multi-threaded programming. Serial execution is pessimistic to the extreme, like holding an exclusive lock on the whole database or partition. Proceeding and checking at commit is the optimistic approach used by SSI.

questions.question: What characterizes optimistic concurrency control, such as serializable snapshot isolation?

options.text: Let transactions proceed and check for violations only at commit
Transactions block on every potential conflict and retry on timeout
Transactions acquire all locks up front and never abort
Transactions run serially but commit optimistically

questions.explanation: Optimistic concurrency control lets transactions continue instead of blocking when something potentially dangerous happens, in the hope that everything turns out fine. When a transaction wants to commit, the database checks whether isolation was violated; if so the transaction is aborted and retried, so only transactions that executed serializably commit. Pessimistic control such as two-phase locking does the opposite and waits as soon as another transaction's lock signals a possible conflict. Optimism works well with low contention and spare capacity, and badly when many transactions conflict and must abort.

questions.question: Under what conditions does optimistic concurrency control perform badly, and why?

options.text: It performs badly under high contention, as many transactions abort
It performs badly only when contention is unusually low
It performs badly only in the presence of long read-only queries
It outperforms pessimistic control under all conditions

questions.explanation: Optimistic control lets transactions run without blocking and aborts those that turn out to conflict. Under high contention, with many transactions accessing the same objects, a large proportion must abort. If the system is already near its maximum throughput, the extra load from retried transactions makes performance even worse, creating a feedback loop.

questions.question: When does optimistic concurrency control tend to perform better than pessimistic control?

options.text: When contention is low and spare capacity can absorb retries
When contention is high, because aborts release resources quickly
When the system is already running near its maximum throughput
When transactions read and write a lot of data over long periods

questions.explanation: If there is enough spare capacity and contention between transactions is not too high, optimistic techniques tend to outperform pessimistic ones because transactions don't wait for locks. Contention can be reduced with commutative atomic operations: concurrent increments to a counter can all be applied without conflict, as long as the transaction doesn't also read the counter. Long read-write transactions are more likely to conflict and abort.

questions.question: What does serializable snapshot isolation add on top of snapshot isolation?

options.text: A way to detect serialization conflicts among writes and decide which to abort
Shared and exclusive locks held until commit, as in two-phase locking
Execution of all write transactions serially on a single thread
Predicate locks that block writers from changing rows that readers have read

questions.explanation: SSI keeps snapshot isolation's reads from a consistent snapshot, which distinguishes it from earlier optimistic techniques. On top of that it tracks when transactions may have acted on outdated reads and, at commit time, aborts transactions whose execution might not be serializable. It does not block readers or writers.

questions.question: In the reasoning behind SSI, what does it mean for a transaction to act on an outdated premise?

options.text: It acted on data it read that then changed before it committed
It wrote some data first and then read back its own uncommitted write
It read the same row twice and got two different committed values
It held a lock on data that it never actually read or wrote

questions.explanation: A premise is a fact that was true when the transaction read it, such as 'there are currently two doctors on call'. Under snapshot isolation, by the time the transaction commits, another transaction may have changed that data, so the premise may no longer be true and the transaction's writes may be invalid. Detecting such situations is how SSI prevents write skew.

questions.question: Why must an SSI database assume that any change to a query's result may invalidate the writes a transaction made afterwards?

options.text: Because it cannot know how the application uses a query's result
Because the application always declares its premises explicitly
Because premises are stored in the transaction log
Because the database can infer application logic from the query

questions.explanation: The database cannot infer every application invariant from SQL results, so it conservatively treats overlapping read-write dependencies as potentially dangerous. That may abort executions that the application knows are harmless.

questions.question: To detect that a transaction may have acted on an outdated premise, which two cases does SSI consider?

options.text: Stale MVCC reads (write before read) and writes affecting prior reads
Dirty reads and dirty writes, both detected before the transaction commits
Deadlocks and phantoms, both of which are detected at commit time
Lost updates and read skew, both detected after the transaction commits

questions.explanation: In the first case, a transaction read from its snapshot while ignoring another transaction's uncommitted write that later committed. In the second, another transaction modifies data after this transaction read it. SSI tracks both kinds of read-write dependency and, at commit, aborts a transaction whose premise has been invalidated by a committed write.

questions.question: Under SSI, two concurrent transactions each read data that the other then writes, so each has acted on a premise the other invalidates. How is this resolved?

options.text: Neither blocks; the first to commit succeeds and the later one aborts at commit
Both commit, because neither transaction blocked the other while running
Both abort immediately as soon as the conflict is noticed
The second transaction blocks until the first commits, then proceeds normally

questions.explanation: SSI records read-write dependencies without blocking either transaction. When the first commits, its write takes effect; when the second tries to commit, the database sees that a write affecting its earlier reads has already committed, so its premise is invalid and it is aborted for the application to retry. Letting both commit would allow write skew.

questions.question: Under SSI, transaction 43 reads from its snapshot while ignoring an uncommitted write by transaction 42. Why doesn't SSI abort 43 as soon as this stale read is detected? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If transaction 43 was a read-only transaction, it wouldn't need to be aborted, because there is no risk of write skew
At the time when transaction 43 makes its read, the database doesn't yet know whether that transaction is going to later perform a write
Transaction 42 may yet abort or may still be uncommitted at the time when transaction 43 is committed, so the read may turn out not to have been stale after all
Aborting the transaction early would violate the durability guarantee

questions.explanation: SSI waits until commit to decide. If 43 turns out to be read-only it never needs aborting, at read time the database doesn't know whether 43 will write, and 42 may still abort or remain uncommitted when 43 commits, so the read may not have been stale after all. Avoiding these unnecessary aborts preserves snapshot isolation's support for long-running reads from a consistent snapshot.

optionExplanations.a: A read-only transaction cannot complete a write-skew cycle because it contributes no write, so aborting it solely for reading an old snapshot would be unnecessary.
optionExplanations.b: At read time the database cannot yet know whether the transaction will later write something that turns the dependency into a dangerous structure.
optionExplanations.c: The apparently conflicting writer may abort, or its commit order may leave no serialization cycle, so SSI waits until the dependency is definitely unsafe.
optionExplanations.d: Durability protects already committed results and does not prohibit aborting an uncommitted transaction early; the delay exists to avoid false-positive aborts.

questions.question: When one transaction writes data that another transaction previously read, what mechanism does SSI borrow from 2PL, and how does SSI change its behavior?

options.text: Index-range locks, which record reads but don't block anyone
Predicate locks, which do block other transactions from writing
Table-level locks, held until the next garbage collection pass
Row locks, held only for the duration of the single statement

questions.explanation: SSI uses index-range markers resembling predicate locks to remember what transactions read. Writers consult those markers to record dependencies, but unlike 2PL they do not block the readers.

questions.question: What does an SSI writer do when it encounters prior read markers?

options.text: It records a dependency instead of blocking those readers
It must block until all readers have committed, exactly like a write lock
It must abort all readers immediately
It need do nothing; readers check at their own commit time

questions.explanation: The index entry records who read the range. A writer consults it and creates dependency metadata; readers and writers continue, and SSI decides at commit whether a dangerous dependency requires an abort.

questions.question: Under SSI, transactions 42 and 43 each read the on-call doctors for shift 1234 and then each updates a doctor's record, so each notifies the other that its earlier read is outdated. Transaction 42 commits first. What happens?

options.text: 42 commits; 43 aborts at commit because 42's write already committed
Both commit, since neither had committed when the notifications were sent
Both abort, since each notified the other of an outdated read
43 commits successfully and 42 is retroactively aborted afterwards

questions.explanation: When a transaction writes, SSI checks which other transactions recently read the affected data and notifies them, acting as a tripwire rather than a blocking lock. Transaction 42 commits first and succeeds because 43's write has not yet taken effect. When 43 tries to commit, 42's conflicting write is already committed, so 43's premise is invalid and it must abort and retry.

questions.question: In SSI, what trade-off governs the granularity at which transactions' reads and writes are tracked?

options.text: Fine tracking is precise but costly; coarse tracking is cheap but over-aborts
Detailed tracking blocks more writers; coarse tracking blocks fewer of them
Detailed tracking retains more snapshot versions; coarse tracking retains fewer
Detailed tracking lengthens lock timeouts; coarse tracking shortens them

questions.explanation: Tracking each transaction's activity in great detail lets the database be precise about which transactions must abort, but the bookkeeping overhead can be significant. Less detailed tracking is faster but may abort more transactions than strictly necessary. PostgreSQL also uses theory to recognize some cases where reading overwritten data still yields a serializable result, reducing unnecessary aborts.

questions.question: Which factor most significantly affects the overall performance of SSI?

options.text: The abort rate, so read-write transactions should be fairly short
Lock wait times, because readers block writers as in two-phase locking
Single-core speed, because all transactions run on one thread
Replication lag, because conflicts are detected on follower replicas

questions.explanation: The abort rate significantly affects SSI's performance: a transaction that reads and writes over a long period is likely to conflict and abort, so read-write transactions should be fairly short, while long read-only transactions may be fine. Unlike 2PL, readers and writers don't block each other, so latency is more predictable, and unlike serial execution, conflict detection can be distributed across machines.

questions.question: Taken as a whole, what role do database transactions play for an application?

options.text: An abstraction hiding certain faults and concurrency problems
A locking mechanism for protecting shared in-memory data structures
A guarantee that each individual write reaches disk before it returns
A performance optimization for batching many separate writes together

questions.explanation: Transactions are an abstraction layer: they let an application pretend that certain concurrency problems and certain hardware and software faults don't exist. A large class of errors is reduced to a simple transaction abort, after which the application just tries again. Locks and logs are implementation mechanisms, and transactions usually cost rather than gain performance.

questions.question: Which applications can most plausibly manage without multi-object transactions?

options.text: Those that only read and write single records
Those that handle money, because each account balance is a single number
Those distributed across many machines, because transactions cannot span nodes
Those with many secondary indexes and much denormalized data

questions.explanation: Not every application is susceptible to every problem: one that only reads and writes single records can probably manage without transactions. For more complex access patterns, such as keeping secondary indexes or denormalized copies in sync, transactions hugely reduce the error cases to consider. Distributed transactions are possible, and handling money usually involves multi-object invariants.

questions.question: Without transactions, what does an application have to handle itself?

options.text: Partial writes from crashes or network faults, plus anomalies from concurrency
Only concurrency problems, since replication handles every fault
Only hardware faults, since the database prevents all concurrency anomalies
Very little, since single-object atomicity covers every multi-object case

questions.explanation: Without transactions, processes crashing, network interruptions, power outages, full disks and unexpected concurrency can all leave data inconsistent, for example denormalized data out of sync with its source. The application must then reason about and repair the effects of complex interacting accesses itself, which is very difficult. Single-object atomicity protects one record but not invariants spanning several.
